## Deuteronomy 19 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1

Moses gave this instruction a few weeks before Israel crossed the Jordan. The conquest was yet to come, but Moses was already applying the law to the conditions they would face once settled in the land. G. Campbell Morgan remarked, “Still with his mind on the fact that the people were coming into the land, Moses made further applications of the laws to the new conditions.” The verb "cut off" (Hebrew *karath*) implies a violent severing; the destruction of the Canaanite nations was God's judgment for their sins. Yet the land itself was a gift of grace to Israel. Though God sovereignly gives the land, Israel remained responsible to "dispossess" the nations and settle. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-19-commentary)

### v. 2

Three cities of refuge were to be set apart in the land west of the Jordan, "in the midst" (centrally located) for easy access. These were anticipated in Exodus 21:12–14, commanded in Numbers 35:9–28, and recorded as established in Joshua 20. Moses had already designated three on the east side: Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan (Deut 4:41–43). The three later established by Joshua were Kedesh (Galilee), Shechem (central hill country), and Hebron (highlands of Judah). These were Levitical cities, chosen because the Levites would be the most impartial judges and their presence could calm the passions of a blood avenger. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-19-commentary)

### v. 3

Israel was to prepare good roads to each city. According to Jewish tradition recorded by Clarke, the roads were made very broad (32 cubits), kept level, and constantly maintained. Bridges were built over rivers and streams so nothing would impede a fleeing manslayer. Rashi notes that at every crossroads, signs reading “Miklot! Miklot!” (“Refuge! Refuge!”) were posted so the fugitive would not lose his way. The land was to be divided into three regions with a city of refuge in each, at roughly equal distances. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/19.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-19.html)

### v. 4

The cities protected only the "manslayer" — someone who killed accidentally, "without knowledge," without prior hatred. Gill notes the Jewish interpretation: if there were no marks of hatred or proofs of enmity during the three days before the incident, it was considered accidental. The manslayer had to remain in the city of refuge until the death of the current high priest (Joshua 20:6) — his life was spared but his liberty was restricted. There were real consequences even for accidental killing. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/19.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-19-commentary)

### v. 5

The case study given illustrates the principle vividly: two men cutting timber together in the woods, and the axe-head flies off the handle and kills the other. The woods were a public place — both men had an equal right to be there. Jewish legal tradition (Mishnah Makkot) specified that what happens "by way of descent" (the axe-head flying off and dropping onto someone) qualifies for refuge, whereas a deliberate throw would not. The key distinction is the absence of intention. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/19.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/)

### v. 6

The "avenger of blood" (Hebrew *goel haddam*) was the kinsman-redeemer (*goel*) — a family member designated to protect the family's honor. His concern was not gathering evidence but avenging the death. The phrase "while his heart is hot" captures the emotional state driving him to pursue before cool deliberation could take place. If the distance to the city was too great, the avenger might overtake and kill a man who "was not deserving of death." The Pulpit Commentary notes that Moses did not seek to abolish the deeply rooted blood-feud system prematurely, but restrained its worst abuses — particularly by distinguishing accidental from intentional killing and establishing the right to a legal trial. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/19.htm)

### v. 7

A summary verse: "This is why I am commanding you to set apart for yourselves three cities." It reinforces that the command is grounded in the need to protect the innocent manslayer. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/19.htm)

### vv. 8–9

God promised that if Israel's territory was enlarged (as sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — see Genesis 15:18, from the Nile to the Euphrates) and if they faithfully kept His commandments, they were to add three more cities. This would bring the total to nine (three east of Jordan, three west, plus three additional). Keil & Delitzsch stress that these three new cities were expressly distinguished from "these three" (v. 9) and cannot be identified with the earlier six. However, the conditions were never fulfilled: Israel never fully kept the law, and even under David and Solomon the extended territory was never brought into actual settled possession — conquered peoples remained in place and were merely tributary. Kalland notes, “Even under David and Solomon, this did not occur; so the third set of cities of refuge was never appointed.” Gill adds that Jewish tradition expected these three additional cities "in the days of the Messiah." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-19.html)

### v. 10

The purpose of the cities was to prevent the shedding of "innocent blood." If an accidental manslayer were killed by the avenger of blood because no refuge was accessible, the guilt of innocent blood would fall upon the whole nation — not only upon the avenger. Keil & Delitzsch explain: "If Israel neglected this duty, it would bring bloodguiltiness upon itself, because it had not done what was requisite to prevent the shedding of innocent blood." Bloodguilt was a corporate responsibility. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-19.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/19.htm)

### vv. 11–13

The cities of refuge were never to be asylums for the guilty. If a man who hated his neighbor, lay in wait, attacked and killed him, then fled to a city of refuge, the elders of his own city were to send for him, retrieve him, and hand him over to the avenger of blood for execution. They were to show "no pity." Merrill notes, "So heinous was murder its penalty was to be inflicted without pity or compassion of any kind. The reason is that humankind is the image of God… therefore murder was deemed to be an assault on God himself." Keil & Delitzsch counter the critical claim (by Riehm, Vater, De Wette) that this transfers judicial inquiry to local elders in contradiction to Numbers 35; they argue the elders were simply performing their duty as local magistrates, not conducting the full trial. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-19.html)

### v. 14

"You must not move your neighbor's boundary marker." These were stones or piles of stones marking family property lines. To move one was to steal land — a violation of the eighth commandment. The law appears here, Ellicott suggests, because land theft was a "most certain incentive to hatred and murder," linking it to the preceding section. But Keil & Delitzsch offer a different rationale: property, by which life is supported, "participates in the sacredness of life itself" — just as sparing fruit trees appears alongside sparing human life in Deuteronomy 20:19–20. The command also carried a spiritual principle: do not lightly remove the "landmarks" (traditions, customs, values) that earlier generations set. Landmarks were regarded as sacred in other ancient cultures too; the Romans made their removal a capital offense. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-19.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-19.html)

### v. 15

The rule from Deuteronomy 17:6 (two or three witnesses required in capital cases) is here extended to all legal matters — civil and criminal. A single witness could not convict anyone of any offense. Guzik notes this protects not only against deliberate lying but also against honest mistake: one witness can be confused or mistaken. Physical evidence (the ancient equivalent of forensic proof) could also serve as a "witness." Gill observes the Jewish exceptions: the case of a woman suspected of adultery and the rite of the beheaded heifer. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/19.htm)

### vv. 16–18

If a false witness arose, both parties — accuser and accused — were to stand "before the LORD, before the priests and the judges." This refers to the supreme court at the central sanctuary (Deuteronomy 17:9), not a local tribunal. The judges were to "investigate thoroughly" (the same phrase used for investigating idolatry in Deuteronomy 13:15). Keil & Delitzsch explain that cases resting on a single witness could not simply be dismissed, so they were referred to the higher tribunal for careful scrutiny. Gill notes the rabbinic ruling that witnesses must be men, not women, and must testify standing. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-19.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/19.htm)

### v. 19

The false witness received the very penalty he intended for the accused — "you shall do to him as he had thought to have done to his brother." This is the *lex talionis* applied to perjury. Clarke comments: "Nothing can be more equitable or proper than this, that if a man endeavour to do any injury to or take away the life of another, on detection he shall be caused to undergo the same evil which he intended for his innocent neighbour." Guzik points out that at Jesus' trial, the false witnesses whose testimony was contradictory (Matthew 26:59–60) should, under this law, have been put to death — since that was the penalty they sought for Jesus. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/)

### v. 20

The public execution of the false witness served as a deterrent: "the rest of the people will hear and be afraid." Guzik observes that modern skepticism about deterrence is contradicted by Scripture: "Weak, delayed, or inconsistent punishment does not deter crime, but effective punishment does." John Trapp added: "Others' woes should be our warnings, others' sufferings our sermons, yea, standing sermons." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/)

### v. 21

"You must show no pity: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot." All the commentators agree this was a principle for the law courts, not for personal vengeance. Thompson: "Far from encouraging vengeance it limits vengeance and stands as a guide for a judge as he fixes a penalty suited to the crime." Guzik notes that Jesus in Matthew 5:38–39 did not say the *lex talionis* was wrong; He condemned the rabbinic abuse that made it an *obligation* to avenge personal insults. This was a law for judges, not for settling personal scores. Gill adds that the Jews interpreted "eye for eye" as monetary compensation — the *price* of an eye for an eye. Keil & Delitzsch note that the same law existed in ancient Egypt (per Diodorus Siculus). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/19.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-19.html)

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Cities of Refuge as a Type of Christ

Nearly all Protestant traditions see the cities of refuge as typifying Christ, but with different emphases:

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasizes that the law itself contains grace. The cities of refuge show God's gracious protection within the law. Significantly, the manslayer's freedom came only at the death of the high priest — "Death was still required to pay for the killing of the innocent person… The high priest’s death was substituted, which points finally to Jesus, the perfect High Priest, who died for all the sins of His people." This reflects a substitutionary atonement emphasis. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/designating-cities-of-refuge — seen in search excerpts)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** Emphasizes the accessibility of Christ. Jesus is the ultimate refuge — available to all, within easy reach, requiring us to stay within His boundaries. The crucial distinction Guzik draws: "while the ancient cities protected only the innocent, Jesus offers refuge to the **guilty** who flee to Him." Precept Austin (citing Grant) adds that the names of the six cities carry spiritual meaning: Kedesh ("holy"), Shechem ("shoulder" — government on His shoulder), Hebron ("fellowship"), Bezer ("fortress"), Ramoth ("high" — exalted), Golan ("joy"). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-19-commentary)

- **Baptist (Gill):** Gill's approach is more restrained typologically, focusing on precise legal distinctions from rabbinic sources (the three-day rule for hatred, women not permitted as witnesses, monetary compensation for "eye for eye"). He notes the Jewish expectation that the three additional cities would come "in the days of the Messiah" — but then states that since Messiah has already come, "all those cities, as they were typical of him, have had their accomplishment in him the antitype." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/19.htm)

### The *Lex Talionis* and Its Application

- **Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** Treats the *lex talionis* as to be applied "without reserve" by the judges. They note it also existed in ancient Egypt, reflecting a common ancient Near Eastern legal principle. No discussion of New Testament modification in the commentary itself — the focus is strictly historical-grammatical. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-19.html)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Explicitly addresses the New Testament tension. Insists Jesus did not reject the *lex talionis* as a principle of justice for courts — only its misapplication to personal relationships. Thompson is quoted: "Jesus' criticism of this law (Matthew 5:38f.) arose from its use to regulate conduct between individuals. He did not reject it as a principle of justice which should operate in the courts of the land." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/)

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** See the *lex talionis* within the broader framework of law and grace. The law shows its gracious character in its protections, yet justice is not sacrificed — the guilty are still punished, and the high priest's death is still required as a substitute, prefiguring Christ. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/designating-cities-of-refuge — seen in search excerpts)

### The Additional Three Cities (vv. 8–9)

- **Lutheran/Keil & Delitzsch:** Emphatically states these three additional cities were *never* established because Israel never fulfilled the conditions. David and Solomon's extension of power to the Euphrates "did not bring the land as far as this river into their actual possession." This is a sober historical reading that ties the promise to conditional obedience. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-19.html)

- **Baptist/Gill:** Notes that the Jews expected these three additional cities "in the days of the Messiah." Gill then declares the Messiah has come and the types are fulfilled in Christ, so the additional three cities are moot. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/19.htm)

- **Pentecostal/Guzik:** Simply notes, citing Kalland, that "even under David and Solomon, this did not occur; so the third set of cities of refuge was never appointed." No eschatological speculation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-19/)

## Other Views

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

### Modern Scholarship

From what was available: the IVP Bible Background Commentary (cited at Precept Austin) notes that the concept of asylum cities was not unique to Israel. Babylonian and Hittite texts speak of sacred spaces where all are protected. The great temple cities of Nippur, Sippar, and Babylon offered special protected status. However, the designation of *entire cities* (not just temple precincts) for asylum was distinctive to Israel. Egyptian tradition applied asylum only to the temple precinct itself — similar to grasping the horns of the altar in Israel (1 Kings 1:50–53). The shift to Levitical cities may have been motivated by a concern to avoid polluting the sanctuary when a lawbreaker grasped the altar. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-19-commentary)

### The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics) on Typology

An interesting moderating voice: "We can scarcely regard them [the cities of refuge] as ordained types of gospel realities, but they certainly furnish valuable illustrations of important gospel truths. To a reader of the New Testament, Christ is suggested by them, and shines through them." This is a more cautious approach than those who treat the cities as divinely intended types. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/19.htm)
